summary: Registers the secret-token URI scheme, intended to help identify authentication tokens. Marking a token with a recognizable prefix makes it easier for tools to spot accidentally exposed secrets, for example in code repositories.

plainLanguage.summary: The secret-token URI scheme gives generated authentication tokens a recognizable form. Tools can scan for it to help detect accidental exposure, but it cannot prevent intentional disclosure.

subtitle: Registers a URI scheme that helps tools identify authentication tokens.

tldr.problem: Accidentally exposed bearer tokens can be used by anyone possessing them, while arbitrary tokens can be hard for tools to identify.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the secret-token URI scheme so generated secrets can use a recognizable prefix that scanning tools can detect.
tldr.outcome: The scheme is intended to help prevent accidental disclosure; it cannot prevent intentional disclosure and is not intended for ephemeral tokens such as CSRF tokens.

sections.title: Why Identify Secret Tokens
sections.content:
A bearer token is a security token that anyone possessing it can use, without proving possession of cryptographic key material. The RFC notes that accidental disclosure of these tokens has caused security incidents, including developers committing access tokens to public repositories.

A recognizable URI scheme can help continuous integration systems or repositories warn about tokens. The RFC intends secret-token URIs for generated secrets such as API keys, not for controlled uses of ephemeral tokens such as CSRF tokens.
sections.plainLanguage: A bearer token can be used by whoever has it. The recognizable scheme is meant to help tools find tokens that were exposed by accident.

sections.title: The URI Format
sections.content:
A secret-token URI consists of the scheme secret-token, a colon and a token with at least one URI character. Disallowed characters, including non-ASCII characters, must first be encoded as UTF-8 and then percent-encoded.

When the URI is generated and later presented for authentication, the entire URI must be used without changes. The RFC gives an example that includes a percent-encoded space.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI begins with secret-token followed by a colon and the token. The full string must stay unchanged when it is used for authentication.

sections.title: Limits of the Scheme
sections.content:
The token syntax allows a token as small as one character, which the RFC says is not recommended. Applications should assess their entropy needs and issue tokens accordingly.

The URI scheme is intended to reduce accidental disclosure, not prevent intentional disclosure. Users may remove the scheme or otherwise obfuscate secret material to evade detection, and the RFC notes that mitigating this can be beyond the reach of the system using the URI.
sections.plainLanguage: The label helps scanning tools, but it does not make a token secret by itself. Users can still remove the label or reveal the token intentionally.
